title: Structures and inhibition of the Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus polymerase.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Queried the RCSB Protein Data Bank (PDB, the public archive of 3D molecular structures) for every entry citing this paper's DOI: exactly 8 entries (9XD4, 9XD5, 9XD6, 9XE6, 9XE7, 9XE9, 9XEC, 9XF9), 7 cryo-electron-microscopy maps at 2.7-3.1 Angstrom and 1 X-ray structure at 1.85 Angstrom, released 2026-05-06. I pulled each entry's metadata (atom counts 5,892-26,455; 1-5 polymer chains each) and downloaded one full coordinate file (9XF9.cif, 717,559 bytes) to confirm the files are real and open.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The abstract only. The paper is paywalled, not in PubMed Central, and Europe PMC reports no supplementary files and no text-mined accessions, so I could not read the Data Availability statement, the methods, or any supplementary table. The claim that 2'-deoxy-2'-fluorocytidine has 'nanomolar cellular potency' and that WXSH0208 inhibits the endonuclease comes from the abstract and is unverified in any file.

a1_downloadable.note: Passes. The 8 PDB/EMDB depositions are public and free; I downloaded 9XF9.cif (718 KB) successfully with no login. The journal article itself is paywalled, but the data is not.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS. There is no label column anywhere. The deposited data is atomic coordinates only. Any prediction target (does a compound inhibit, at what concentration, is a residue a contact) would have to be constructed by reading gels and dose-response curves out of paywalled figures and re-deriving contacts from the structures.

a3_inputs_present.note: Protein and RNA sequences and full 3D coordinates are present in the mmCIF files; the two inhibitors are present as chemical components with defined structures. Inputs are not the problem here.

a4_units_stated.note: FAILS by absence. There is no measured quantity in the deposited files to carry units. Resolution is in Angstroms, but that is a property of the experiment, not a prediction target. The potency numbers that would carry units (nanomolar) exist only inside the paywalled figures.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS decisively, and this is the killer. I counted exactly 8 deposited structures, verified by DOI search against RCSB. The checklist floor is ~1,500 labelled rows, or ~400 for classification. 8 is three orders of magnitude short. Counting individual amino acids or atoms as rows would not fix this: they are not independent examples.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~6 MB total for all 8 coordinate files; a few GB if the raw cryo-EM maps were also pulled
a6_fits_laptop.note: Passes trivially. The coordinate files are tiny. Size was never the issue.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The 8 PDB entries citing this DOI are consistent with an abstract describing apo, 5'-RNA-bound, 3'-RNA-bound, several elongating complexes, and one inhibitor-bound endonuclease. No contradiction found, though I could not read the Data Availability statement to cross-check.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAILS for want of a label. There is no measurement to trace. A structure is a model fitted to a density map, so even 'the coordinates' are partly an inference, not a direct physical readout; using contacts derived from them as labels would be learning the depositors' modelling choices.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available: with 8 structures and no measured outcome column there is nothing a model could be trained to claim.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use viral polymerase structure to predict which small molecules block Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus replication.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on the 8 deposited three-dimensional structures of the Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus Large (L) protein, the enzyme that copies the virus's genome, including two of them with a drug bound. 8 examples, verified by counting PDB entries.
plain_idea.predict: Whether, and how strongly, a given compound inhibits this polymerase. The true answer would come from laboratory enzyme assays and cell-based potency measurements, which in this paper were done for only two compounds and reported only inside paywalled figures.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever has no licensed drug and is a World Health Organization priority pathogen, so antiviral chemists would use a reliable potency predictor. But this paper supplies structures, not the measurements such a model needs.

label_elsewhere.sources: Not assessed in detail because the verdict is reject. Compound potency against viral polymerases does exist in ChEMBL and PubChem, but nothing in this paper's deposited data joins to it.
label_elsewhere.join_key: none present in the deposited files
label_elsewhere.why: This paper contributes no labelled items that could be matched against an external potency resource.

ml_idea: None viable from this paper. The only machine-readable output is 8 atomic-coordinate files. The structures are genuinely valuable as *input features* for someone else's project (for example, adding the Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus polymerase to a structure-based virtual screening benchmark, or using the two inhibitor-bound sites as docking targets), but that project's labels and training data would have to come entirely from elsewhere, so it is not a project this paper supports.

effort.compute_note: Working-set size measured: one downloaded coordinate file was 718 KB, and all 8 entries together are roughly 6 MB. No training estimate is meaningful because there is no training set.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the deposited entries. One RCSB search by DOI returns 8, which is already fatal; it took under a minute and should always be the first thing done on a structural-biology paper.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A5 by three orders of magnitude: the paper's entire machine-readable output is 8 deposited structures (7 cryo-electron-microscopy, 1 X-ray), verified by DOI search and one file download, against a floor of ~1,500 labelled rows. It also fails A2, A4 and A8 because there is no measured outcome column at all. This is excellent structural biology and the structures will be useful as docking targets for other people's screening projects, but a structure paper with 8 depositions and two tested compounds cannot be the data source for a machine learning project. The paper being paywalled with no supplement in PubMed Central compounds the problem: the only quantitative measurements it contains are locked inside figures.
